chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hisham ibn Salim and Muhammad ibn Humran, from Al-Walid ibn Sabih, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Zurara met me coming out from his presence. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Walid! Do you not wonder at Zurara? He asked me about the 'amal (office/position) of these people. What did he want? Did he want me to say 'No' to him so he could report that from me?' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'O Walid! When did the Shia ask about their 'amal? Rather, the Shia used to say: 'One can eat from their food, and drink from their drink, and find shade under their shadow.' When did the Shia ask about this?'

key_terms.الشِّيعَةُ: The Shia, referring to the followers of the Imams
key_terms.زُرَارَةُ: Zurara ibn A'yan, a prominent companion and scholar

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the Shia's changing attitude towards religious office and authority?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses this anecdote to highlight the evolution of Shia political consciousness, contrasting the early era of passive proximity and sustenance with the later period of active inquiry into administrative roles (wilayah). This shift reflects the community's growing need to understand the practical application of religious authority during the transition from the quietist approach to the era of greater political engagement under the Umayyads and Abbasids. The humor underscores the natural progression of the faithful from seeking spiritual closeness to seeking structural clarity in governance.
